articles.title: The Gold Rings of Seoul
articles.dek: In the winter of 1998, millions of Koreans handed over their wedding bands to save their country. The first readers of Hebrews had once given up even more, and the writer wanted them to remember why.
articles.quote: Your confidence before God is the one possession no one can carry down the stairs, and the only way to lose it is to set it down yourself.
articles.body:
In January 1998, the lines outside banks in Seoul stretched around city blocks in the freezing cold. South Korea was in deep trouble. The Asian financial crisis that had begun in Thailand the summer before had swept north, the won had lost about half its value, and companies that had seemed as permanent as mountains were collapsing one after another. The government had been forced to accept a rescue package from the International Monetary Fund worth some fifty-eight billion dollars, and many Koreans felt it as a national humiliation. So ordinary people did something no economist had asked them to do. They went home, opened their drawers and jewelry boxes, and brought their gold to the nation.

Filipinos who lived through that same crisis, when the peso tumbled and the price of everything climbed, can picture what this meant. Gold in an Asian home is seldom just metal. It is the wedding band slipped on in front of the whole family, the necklace a lola set aside for her eldest granddaughter, the tiny ring given to a Korean baby at the doljanchi, the first-birthday celebration, as a wish for a long and blessed life. People handed over all of it. Couples gave their wedding rings, athletes gave their medals, and widows gave the rings their late husbands had placed on their fingers. Within a few months, roughly three and a half million people contributed about 227 tons of gold. When reporters asked why, the answers kept returning to one idea: the country mattered more than the ring. South Korea finished repaying its IMF loans in August 2001, years ahead of schedule.

Nobody standing in those lines would have described what they did as a loss. They knew exactly what they were holding onto, and that knowledge made the giving almost glad. That is the very kind of memory the writer of Hebrews asks his readers to recover in chapter 10.

We do not know for certain who wrote Hebrews, but we know a good deal about the people who first received it. They were believers, most likely Jewish Christians, who had come to faith in Jesus and paid dearly for it. Many scholars think they lived in or near Rome, and the suffering the letter recalls may connect with the emperor Claudius expelling Jews from the city around AD 49, an event Luke mentions in Acts 18:2. Years had passed since then. The first fire had burned down to embers, some of them were drifting away from the gatherings of the church (Hebrews 10:25), and a few were wondering whether slipping quietly back into the familiar rituals of the synagogue might simply be easier.

So the writer takes them back. Picture a small house church in a crowded Roman neighborhood, where word has spread that the family on the second floor worships a crucified Jew. One afternoon the shouting begins in the street. Neighbors they once traded bread with are mocking them in the market, and the Greek word the writer uses in verse 33, theatrizō, means to be put on stage as a public spectacle, the way a crowd stares at a show. Then men come up the stairs and start carrying things out: the table, the lamps, the bedding, the clay jars of oil, perhaps the family's small purse of coins. Hebrews remembers how these believers answered. They walked across the city to visit friends who had been thrown into prison, bringing food, since Roman prisons often left inmates to be fed by whoever cared for them. And when they came home to bare rooms, they were glad.

"You suffered along with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, because you knew that you yourselves had better and lasting possessions. So do not throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded." (Hebrews 10:34–35)

The writer explains their joy in a single phrase: they "knew that you yourselves had better and lasting possessions" (10:34). The Greek word for possessions here, hyparxis, is ordinary property language, the kind of word you might find on a household inventory. The writer is telling them that their real inventory had been kept somewhere the mob could never reach. Like the Korean families who looked at a wedding band and saw something greater than gold, these believers looked at an empty room and counted what no one could carry down the stairs.

Then comes the command: "do not throw away your confidence." The verb, apoballō, pictures flinging something off, and it is the same word Mark uses when blind Bartimaeus throws his cloak aside to run to Jesus (Mark 10:50). The word for confidence, parrēsia, is the one the writer used at the start of this very section: "since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus" (Hebrews 10:19). In the Greek world, parrēsia was a citizen's freedom to speak openly and without fear in the public assembly. In Hebrews it becomes the freedom of a forgiven child to walk straight into God's presence. For centuries only the high priest could pass through the curtain into the Most Holy Place, and only once a year, but now, verse 20 says, Jesus has opened "a new and living way" through his own body.

One way to read this passage, then, is to see that the treasure these believers were in danger of losing was the one thing their persecutors had never managed to touch. The neighbors took the table and the lamps, and their access to God stayed perfectly safe through all of it. Your confidence before God is the one possession no one can carry down the stairs, and the only way to lose it is to set it down yourself. That usually happens slowly, through weariness, the way a tired traveler finally lets a heavy cloak slide off by the roadside. This is why the writer's remedy is memory. The people who once let go of everything for Christ were the same people now tempted to let go of Christ for a little peace, and he wants them to remember who they were.

Many of us know that drift from the inside. Faith often burns brightest when the cost is high and the stakes are plain. Perhaps you came to Christ in a season of trouble, prayed your way through a parent's illness, or gave generously when you had little to spare. Then the crisis passed, the years settled into routine, and the old fire became a memory you seldom visit. The danger in that season tends to arrive as a gradual loosening of the grip, missing one Sunday and then several, praying less because nothing feels urgent, until the cloak is lying in the dust and you hardly remember dropping it.

The writer's medicine works as well in Manila as it did in Rome. Take ten quiet minutes today to remember your own earlier days, and write down one specific time God carried you and one thing you gave up for him that you have never regretted. Then do what verses 24 and 25 ask and "consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds," perhaps by sending a short message to someone who has been missing from your church lately, telling them simply that you remember them and that you are glad they belong.

The gold rings of Seoul covered only a small part of Korea's debt, yet they showed the world a people who knew what they truly owned. "You need to persevere," Hebrews 10:36 says, "so that when you have done the will of God, you will receive what he has promised." Your welcome into God's presence was bought at a price far greater than any gold, by the blood of Jesus himself, and it is yours to keep close today. The writer closes this chapter with a pastor's warm certainty about his people, and he would say it about you too: "we do not belong to those who shrink back and are destroyed, but to those who have faith and are saved" (Hebrews 10:39).

articles.title: The Little Sanctuary on a Borrowed Sidewalk
articles.dek: The people of Jerusalem were sure the exiles had lost God when they lost the temple. In Ezekiel 11, God answers that he had moved in with them.
articles.quote: Wherever you have been scattered this week, God has already gone ahead of you to be your sanctuary there.
articles.illustration: Filipino helpers' Sundays in Hong Kong
articles.body:
On Sundays in Hong Kong, the banking district of Central fills with Filipinos. Many of the roughly 200,000 Filipino domestic workers who keep the city's households running spend their one day off sitting on folded cardboard and plastic mats under the glass towers. By mid-morning the pavement beneath the HSBC building and around Statue Square is crowded with rice in foil trays and adobo packed in reused ice-cream tubs, and you can hear Tagalog, Ilocano and Bisaya over the traffic. A woman trims a friend's hair while another reads a letter from her child in Iloilo, and in one corner a circle of women in matching shirts opens their Bibles and starts a worship song you could hear in any barangay chapel back home.

Tourists sometimes call it a giant picnic, and the women laugh at that, because they know it is more. For one day a week, a strip of concrete in a foreign city becomes a piece of home. Many of them are thousands of kilometers from their parish and their families, yet they will tell you that some of their sweetest seasons of prayer happened right there, on a borrowed sidewalk, among friends who had become family. More than twenty-five centuries ago, God said something through the prophet Ezekiel that those women would recognize at once.

In 592 BC Ezekiel was living as an exile in Babylon. He had been taken from Jerusalem five years earlier with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Judah's leading families, and he now lived beside the Kebar canal, far from the temple he had been trained to serve as a priest. Chapter 8 opens in his house, with the elders of Judah sitting in front of him, when "the hand of the Sovereign LORD came on me there" (Ezekiel 8:1). In a vision, God lifts him by the hair and carries him back to Jerusalem to see what is going on inside the temple.

What he sees is heartbreaking. An idol stands at the north gate. In a hidden room, seventy elders burn incense to images of animals painted on the walls. Women sit weeping for Tammuz, a Babylonian fertility god, and twenty-five men turn their backs on God's sanctuary to bow toward the rising sun. Their excuse shows how far they had drifted: "The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land" (Ezekiel 8:12). Then, in chapters 9 and 10, Ezekiel watches the unthinkable. The shining glory of God, the visible sign of his presence that had filled Solomon's temple, rises from its place, moves to the threshold, pauses at the east gate (Ezekiel 10:18–19), and prepares to leave.

You would expect the people still living in Jerusalem to be terrified, but they were smug. Their leaders had a saying: "This city is a pot, and we are the meat in it" (Ezekiel 11:3). Their meaning was that they were the choice cuts, kept safe inside the pot, while the exiles had been thrown out like scraps. They said it plainly about Ezekiel's neighbors in Babylon: "They are far away from the LORD; this land was given to us as our possession" (Ezekiel 11:15). In their theology, being close to God meant living near the building. The exiles had lost the building, so everyone assumed they had lost God too.

Then God answers, and his answer is one of the tenderest verses in the whole book.

"Although I sent them far away among the nations and scattered them among the countries, yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries where they have gone." (Ezekiel 11:16)

The Hebrew phrase behind "for a little while I have been a sanctuary" is miqdash me'at. Miqdash is the ordinary word for a holy place, the same word used for the temple itself. Me'at means "little," and scholars have long noted that it can be read two ways: "for a little while" or "in a small measure." Jewish teachers loved the second reading so much that the Talmud later used this verse to describe the humble synagogues and prayer houses the scattered people built wherever they lived. In each foreign town, the meeting room became a miqdash me'at, a little sanctuary, because God had promised to be one.

The timing in the passage makes the promise even more moving. At the very moment the glory of God is lifting from the grand temple in Jerusalem, God tells the people in exile that he himself has become their sanctuary. One way to read Ezekiel 8 through 11 is as a story about where God chose to be found. The people who lived next to the gold and cedar had turned their backs on him, while the people sitting in a refugee's house by a Babylonian canal had God sitting with them. Ezekiel's first vision of God's glory, back in chapter 1, came to him right there in Babylon, years before this one. God was already among the exiles when the people back home were calling them forgotten.

God does not stop with comfort. In the next breath he promises, "I will give them an undivided heart and put a new spirit in them; I will remove from them their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 11:19), and he ends with the line that sums up the whole covenant: "They will be my people, and I will be their God" (Ezekiel 11:20). The rest of Scripture follows the same path. John writes that the Word "made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14), and Jesus tells a Samaritan woman that true worshipers will worship in the Spirit and in truth, whether on her mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). God keeps moving toward the people others have written off.

This speaks to a lot of Filipino homes. Nearly every family has someone abroad, or someone who moved to Manila for work, or someone sent away by circumstances they never chose. If that is you, you may sometimes feel the way those exiles felt, a little behind spiritually because you are far from your home church, your lola's rosary, the chapel where you were baptized. Ezekiel 11:16 is God's direct reply to that fear. A night-shift desk, a dormitory bunk in Riyadh or a cardboard mat in Central can all become a miqdash me'at, because the sanctuary is God himself, and he goes wherever his people go.

The passage also gently warns those of us who stayed. The Jerusalem crowd had a habit of measuring other people's faith by their distance from the right place, and families can slide into the same habit without meaning to. We say of a cousin who stopped attending Mass, or a sibling who moved abroad and changed churches, that they have drifted. Before we say it, we can remember that God was building a sanctuary among the very people the insiders had dismissed, and that his harshest words in these chapters were for the ones who felt safe inside the pot.

One concrete way to live this today is to treat the place where you actually are as holy ground. Before you start work, quietly name the room you are in and say, "Lord, be my little sanctuary here." Then think of one person far from home, a kababayan abroad or a relative the family rarely mentions, and send them a message that says God has not forgotten them. You might be the person who reminds them that the Lord is closer than they think.

Those women singing under the towers of Central understand Ezekiel better than many of us who sit in comfortable pews. Wherever you have been scattered this week, God has already gone ahead of you to be your sanctuary there. Your sidewalk, your hospital corridor or your small rented room may be exactly where he has chosen to meet you, and he intends to stay.

articles.title: The Bible on a String
articles.dek: In a camp built to break people, two sisters kept a small book alive, and it kept them alive. A psalm writer knew that secret centuries before Ravensbrück.
articles.quote: The word you delight in today is the word that will hold you on the day you cannot hold yourself.
articles.body:
In September 1944, a fifty-two-year-old watchmaker named Corrie ten Boom stood in a line of prisoners at Ravensbrück, a concentration camp for women north of Berlin. She had been arrested with her family in Haarlem, in the Netherlands, for hiding Jewish neighbors in their home. Under her dress, on a string around her neck, hung a small cloth pouch, and inside it was a little Bible. The guards were searching every woman in the line, and Corrie knew that if they found it, the book would be taken from her.

She prayed as she inched forward. In her memoir, The Hiding Place, she recalls the guard running her hands over the woman in front of her and the woman behind her, and passing over Corrie as though she were invisible. The Bible came through. In the weeks that followed, in the crowded and flea-ridden Barracks 28, Corrie and her older sister Betsie held evening readings under a dim bulb. They read aloud in Dutch, and other prisoners translated each verse into German, then into French, Polish, Russian, and Czech, so that the words moved from bunk to bunk like water passed along a line of buckets.

The sisters later discovered why the guards seldom came in to stop them: the soldiers refused to enter a barracks so full of fleas. Betsie had thanked God for those fleas when Corrie could not bring herself to, and that small, strange mercy became one of the most loved parts of their story. Betsie died in Ravensbrück that December. Before she did, she told her sister something Corrie would repeat to audiences around the world for more than thirty years: "There is no pit so deep that He is not deeper still."

Corrie was released at the end of that month through what she always believed was a clerical error, and she went home thin and nearly penniless. When people asked how she had endured, she kept pointing them to the God who had met her in that book. Centuries before her, a psalm writer had put the same testimony into one sentence.

That sentence sits in Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible. Its 176 verses form an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with all eight lines of each stanza beginning with the same letter. It reads a little like a child working through the alphabet, except that every letter becomes a prayer. Almost every verse mentions God's word under one name or another, such as law, statutes, precepts, commands, or promise. The author is unnamed, but he tells us plainly that he was under pressure. "The arrogant mock me unmercifully," he writes, "but I do not turn from your law" (Psalm 119:51), and elsewhere, "Though the wicked bind me with ropes, I will not forget your law" (Psalm 119:61).

Today's stanza, the one marked by the letter lamed, opens exactly halfway through the psalm. Just before it, the writer sounds almost spent. "My eyes fail, looking for your promise," he says, and "I am like a wineskin in the smoke" (Psalm 119:82–83), picturing a leather bottle hung near a fire until it turns black and brittle. He admits his enemies "almost wiped me from the earth" (Psalm 119:87). Then, at the turning point of the whole poem, he lifts his eyes: "Your word, LORD, is eternal; it stands firm in the heavens" (Psalm 119:89). The earth endures because God established it (v. 90), and all things serve him (v. 91). From that high ground he looks back over his own suffering and writes this:

"If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction." (Psalm 119:92)

The Hebrew word translated "delight" is sha'ashu'im, and it carries the warmth of play. It comes from a root used for the absorbed, happy pleasure of a small child, the kind of joy a toddler takes in a favorite thing and a parent takes in that toddler. Isaiah uses the related verb when he pictures a peaceful kingdom in which "the infant will play near the cobra's den" (Isaiah 11:8). Jeremiah uses this very noun when God speaks with aching tenderness about his wandering people: "Is not Ephraim my dear son, the child in whom I delight?" (Jeremiah 31:20).

One way to read verse 92, then, is as a confession of love. The word that kept the psalmist alive was a word he had enjoyed. He had returned to it the way a child returns to something beloved, again and again, for the plain pleasure of it, and he had been doing that long before the affliction came. When the dark season arrived, the delight he had cultivated in ordinary days became the thing that held him. The verb for "perished," 'abad, comes from the same root he uses in the psalm's final verse: "I have strayed like a lost sheep" (Psalm 119:176). Without that daily delight, he says, he would have been lost in his trouble, the way a sheep is lost on a hillside at night.

The ten Boom family lived this long before the war. For decades their father, Casper, read Scripture aloud at the table after breakfast and again in the evening, while the family and whoever happened to be visiting listened. By the time his daughters reached Ravensbrück, the Bible was an old companion whose voice they knew well. The camp revealed how deep that love already ran, and the habit of a dining table in Haarlem became the strength of Barracks 28.

This gives the rest of us great hope, because delight can be grown. Most of us reach for God's word hardest when life falls apart, and he is gracious to meet us there. Yet the psalmist shows us a gentler, wiser path, in which we learn to love these pages in the calm seasons so that they are familiar when the storm comes. The word you delight in today is the word that will hold you on the day you cannot hold yourself.

The stanza adds two more comforts. In verse 94 the writer prays, "Save me, for I am yours." He rests his whole plea on belonging, and that is a prayer anyone can pray, including on the days when our devotion feels thin. Then he closes with this: "To all perfection I see a limit, but your commands are boundless" (Psalm 119:96). He has watched the finest things in life reach their edges, as every human achievement eventually does. God's word, by contrast, is literally "exceedingly broad" in Hebrew (rechabah me'od). The same family of words appears when David sings, "He brought me out into a spacious place; he rescued me because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). Corrie lived in a cramped, overcrowded barracks, yet in God's word she found room to breathe.

You might begin tonight with something small. Read Psalm 119:89–96 slowly before you sleep, and choose the one line that warms you most. Write it on a card for your wallet or set it as your phone's lock screen, and return to it during the commute or the long shift abroad, the way a child returns to a favorite song. Over weeks and months that line will become yours, and the God who spoke it will grow more familiar still.

Corrie ten Boom spent the rest of her life traveling to more than sixty countries, telling people that God's love reaches into the deepest places. She had seen that love in a flea-ridden barracks, where a little Bible passed from hand to hand. The same word stands firm in the heavens today (Psalm 119:89), and it is waiting for you to delight in it, one small verse at a time.

articles.title: The Money That Grew Wings
articles.dek: An ancient proverb says riches fly away like an eagle. A young Oxford teacher took that seriously and decided ahead of time where his money would land.
articles.quote: Wealth was always going to fly; generosity simply chooses where it lands.
articles.body:
In the winter of 1731, a young Oxford lecturer named John Wesley had just finished buying some pictures for his rooms when a chambermaid knocked at his door. It was a bitterly cold day, and he could see that she was wearing only a thin linen gown. He reached into his pocket to give her something for a warmer coat and found that he had almost nothing left, because the pictures had taken it.

Wesley later wrote that a question rose in him that he could not shake. Would his Master say, "Well done, good and faithful servant," to a man who had decorated his walls with money that might have kept this poor woman from the cold? He answered that question with a plan. His income that year was about thirty pounds, and he found he could live on twenty-eight, so he gave away two. The next year his income doubled to sixty pounds, and he kept living on twenty-eight and gave away thirty-two. As the figure climbed to ninety and then to one hundred twenty, the amount he lived on stayed close to where it had started, and everything above it went to the poor, to prisoners, to orphans, and to struggling preachers.

Decades later, when his books and preaching had made him one of the best-known men in England, Wesley wrote a line in a letter that sounds almost playful: "Money never stays with me. It would burn me if it did. I throw it out of my hands as soon as possible, lest it should find a way into my heart." He had learned early what a Hebrew teacher had written nearly three thousand years before him, that money has a habit of leaving. Wesley decided that if it was going to leave anyway, he would choose where it went.

That old teacher's words sit in Proverbs 23, inside a section that begins back in Proverbs 22:17 and calls itself the "thirty sayings" of the wise (Proverbs 22:20). These sayings read like a training manual for a young man being prepared for public life, someone who would one day stand near power and handle other people's money. So the chapter opens at a royal table. "When you sit to dine with a ruler, note well what is before you" (Proverbs 23:1). Picture the young official at his first state banquet, the platters arriving one after another, roasted meats and honeyed breads he has never tasted at home. The teacher leans over with a startling piece of advice: "put a knife to your throat if you are given to gluttony" (Proverbs 23:2). It is a vivid exaggeration, the kind a mentor uses so you never forget it, and it means that you should restrain your appetite with real force.

The reason follows at once: "Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive" (Proverbs 23:3). A ruler's generosity often comes with strings. The feast may be a way of buying loyalty, or of watching how a newcomer behaves when he is given more than he needs. Then the teacher widens the lens from the plate in front of the young man to the whole direction of his life.

"Do not wear yourself out to get rich; do not trust your own cleverness. Cast but a glance at riches, and they are gone, for they will surely sprout wings and fly off to the sky like an eagle." (Proverbs 23:4–5)

The Hebrew of verse 5 holds a small piece of wordplay that English translations struggle to carry. The phrase "cast but a glance" is built on the verb 'uph, which means "to fly." Read very literally, the teacher asks, "Will you let your eyes fly toward it?" A few words later the same verb returns, and this time it is the riches that fly, sprouting wings and soaring off like an eagle. The picture is of a chase in which your eyes dart toward wealth and the wealth darts away, so that the faster you lunge, the faster it rises.

Historians have found a close cousin of this saying in an Egyptian wisdom text called the Instruction of Amenemope, which warns that riches "have made themselves wings like geese" and flown to the sky. Many scholars think Israel's wise men knew and adapted that older teaching, which tells us that people in many nations had already watched fortunes vanish. The Hebrew version chooses a sharper bird. A goose can be chased across a field, but an eagle climbs higher and faster than any person can follow, and once it is gone, it is gone.

Verse 4 explains why we keep chasing anyway. The word for "wear yourself out" (yaga') describes toil that leaves a person exhausted, the kind of labor that never quite arrives at rest. And the phrase "do not trust your own cleverness" uses binah, the ordinary Hebrew word for understanding. The teacher is gently warning against the confident belief that we are smart enough to outrun the wings, that with one more sideline, one more contract, or one more year abroad we will finally catch hold of something that stays.

Here the gospel shines a light the young official at the banquet could only glimpse. Jesus took this same truth and gave it a destination: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moths and vermin destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:19–20). Paul goes deeper still, pointing to what Christ himself did with his riches: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Son of God let go of everything so that we could be given an inheritance that has no wings at all. When you know you are already rich in Christ, you can stop wearing yourself out, and generosity becomes a glad response to grace rather than a grim duty.

Filipinos understand the eagle in this proverb better than most. This week the peso slipped to yet another record low, and many families felt their savings shrink without spending a single centavo. Many of us also know a parent abroad who has worked through holidays for years, or a relative who poured everything into a business that disappeared overnight. Proverbs does not shame anyone for working hard or for wanting to provide. It simply tells the truth that money is a guest, and a guest always leaves eventually.

Wesley's quiet discipline offers a practical way to live with that truth. You might sit down this week, perhaps with your spouse or family, and name a simple amount that is enough for your household in this season, your own version of his twenty-eight pounds. Then decide now, before the next raise, bonus, or remittance arrives, what portion of anything above that line will go to God's work and to someone in need. Making the decision ahead of time means the money's flight is already planned, and it lands in a church pantry, a scholarship, or a neighbor's hospital bill instead of quietly disappearing into things that will not matter next year.

Paul gave Timothy instructions for wealthy believers that fit this proverb well. He told him to command them "not to be arrogant nor to put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain, but to put their hope in God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment" (1 Timothy 6:17). That last phrase deserves to be held close, because the same God who warns us about winged riches is the One who delights to provide for his children. Wealth was always going to fly; generosity simply chooses where it lands. Hold today's money with an open hand, rest in the riches you already have in Christ, and let the next thing that leaves your wallet carry warmth to someone standing in the cold.
